card.tagline: A 1981 hip-hop dance from New York City characterized by jerky, rhythmic body movements.
card.profile: The Harlem shake is a hip-hop dance originating in 1981 in the Harlem neighborhood of New York City. Created by Albert Leopold Boyce, known as 'Al B', the dance features distinct, jerky arm and shoulder movements. It gained mainstream popularity in 2001 through music videos and remains a distinct cultural practice separate from the 2013 internet meme of the same name.
card.insight: The dance was originally called 'The Albee' after its creator, Al B, who claimed the movement was inspired by the restricted motion of ancient Egyptian mummies.

card.profile_long:
The Harlem shake emerged in 1981 within the Harlem neighborhood of New York City. Initially known as 'The Albee' after its creator, Albert Leopold Boyce—a local figure known as Al B—the dance was frequently performed during breaks at the Entertainer's Basketball Classic at Rucker Park. As the dance spread beyond its original neighborhood, it was renamed the Harlem shake. Al B, who passed away in 2006, described the movement as a 'drunken shake' and often attributed its inspiration to the limited mobility of ancient Egyptian mummies, who could only shake due to being wrapped in bandages. Other accounts suggest the dance may have been influenced by the Ethiopian dance Eskista or the movements of Al B's mother, Sandra Boyce.

The dance remained a regional staple for two decades before entering the mainstream in 2001. Its visibility surged following its inclusion in the music video for G. Dep's 'Let's Get It', which featured children performing the steps. This period marked a peak in the dance's popularity within hip-hop culture, with appearances in music videos by artists such as Jadakiss and G. Dep. The dance also received lyrical mentions in tracks by Cam'ron and Missy Elliott. By 2006, the Harlem shake had influenced the evolution of other popular movements, most notably 'The Chicken Noodle Soup', which gained widespread attention through DJ Webstar and Young B.

Technically, the Harlem shake is defined by jerky, rhythmic movements of the arms and shoulders. It is a style of hip-hop dance that emphasizes a specific, shaking quality. Despite the global viral phenomenon in 2013 surrounding a song titled 'Harlem Shake' by Baauer, the dance performed in those viral videos is distinct from the original Harlem shake created by Al B. The original dance remains a specific cultural artifact of Harlem's hip-hop history, distinct from the internet meme that later co-opted its name.

steps.name: Harlem Shake Shoulders
steps.description: Alternating shoulder pops with loose body posture and hip opposition.

common_mistakes: Being too stiff and trying to lock up instead of staying loose

lessons.distinctive_method: Emphasizing the mental cue of staying loose and comparing shoulders to a key and lock mechanism.
what_works: Clear demonstration of shoulder isolation and body looseness
what_hinders: Quick transitions between talking and demonstrating without formal counts

evidence.observation: Instructor stands facing front explaining shoulder movement using his hands to point to the right and left shoulders.
